blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
On-policy distillation (OPD) ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) trains a student on
its own rollouts, with each token scored by a frozen teacher. It combines
the dense per-token supervision of classical knowledge
distillation ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) with on-policy sampling
that avoids the train/test mismatch of teacher-generated data.
Dense teacher feedback suggests that OPD may learn from fewer rollouts than outcome-reward RL such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) .
Its promise is sharpest on hard problems: when the student rarely finds a correct answer, outcome-reward GRPO has little positive signal, while the teacher can still supervise every generated token.
Yet that supervision requires a teacher forward pass on every training token, and longer responses raise the cost further.
Fewer rollouts or optimizer steps therefore need not mean fewer FLOPs. Can OPD reach the same accuracy as GRPO with fewer training FLOPs? Existing efficiency reports use GPU-hours, gradient-step ratios, or partial FLOPs comparisons, leaving the matched-FLOPs comparison unresolved.
To our knowledge, no prior work systematically compares OPD and GRPO
at matched training FLOPs (§ 2 ; Appendix A ).

blocks.en:
In this work, we focus on systematically comparing reverse-KL OPD with GRPO by tracking held-out task performance against cumulative training FLOPs.
Our experiments vary data difficulty, student and teacher sizes and initializations, training domain, thinking mode, distillation objective, and the RL framework.
With off-the-shelf post-trained teachers, GRPO generally achieves higher accuracy at a fixed FLOP budget.
Reducing OPD to one rollout per prompt is the one change that lets an external teacher outperform GRPO, and only on single-domain math; the advantage disappears on code and multi-domain training (Appendix I ).
To our surprise, this even holds in the subset that should
intuitively favour OPD most: a small student that barely solves
( mean@32 = 0 {=}0 ) paired with a large teacher that solves well
( mean@32 > 0.6 {>}0.6 ), where GRPO’s outcome reward is very weak and
dense per-token supervision should matter most (§ 4.1 ).
External-teacher OPD consistently inflates response length until it reaches the maximum length, increasing the FLOPs paid per step (Appendix E ).

We next ask whether the teacher’s training history changes the result.
Recent work reports that GRPO-training the teacher before distillation can
help the student learn better ( Li et al., 2026 ) .
Building on this evidence, we compare external thinking models, further-GRPO-trained thinking models, and GRPO-trained base models at or above the student’s size.
Among the teachers tested, OPD consistently recovers the teacher’s accuracy only when the teacher is a GRPO checkpoint of the student.
In particular, in our math setting, OPD with one rollout per prompt matches that checkpoint’s accuracy with 50 50 × \times fewer distillation-stage FLOPs ( 6 6 × \times at the default 8-rollout-per-prompt setting) than the eight-rollout GRPO training needs to reach the same accuracy.
We further find such observation generalizes across model sizes, domains, and model families.
When using Olmo-3-7B-Instruct-SFT on math, we are surprised to find self-GRPO OPD can lead to a student outperforming teacher substantially by 11% absolute score.

blocks.en:
However, distilling from the student’s own GRPO checkpoint reveals a
paradox: on a single domain, why distill when you already have the
GRPO-trained model?
The 50 50 × \times ratio counts only distillation: the GRPO run has already produced the desired single domain model, so distilling it back into the base student adds cost.
Consider math and code: separate GRPO runs produce two specialists, but neither checkpoint can serve both domains.
This is where multi-teacher OPD has a distinct compute-efficiency opportunity: it can consolidate the GRPO specialists into the multi-domain model neither provides, with only a small additional distillation cost.
The decisive compute test is whether the cost of training those experts and consolidating them via distillation beats that of joint GRPO on the same data mix.
Recent open-source models ( Yang et al., 2026d ; Team et al., 2026 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ; Kimi Team, 2026 ) use this recipe, but leave that full-pipeline comparison unmeasured.
Multi-teacher OPD combines the per-domain GRPO experts into a single student model that recovers their performance, with distillation adding only 5.2 true % 5.2\text{true}\mathrm{\%} (two domains) and 8.0 true % 8.0\text{true}\mathrm{\%} (four domains) to the specialists’ training FLOPs.
Counting both stages, the two-domain pipeline reaches joint GRPO’s accuracy on the same data mix with 42 true % 42\text{true}\mathrm{\%} fewer total FLOPs.
On both two-domain and four-domain settings, joint GRPO does not even reach the merged student’s performance within the tested budget.

blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Many recent methods modify the canonical reverse-KL objective for external-teacher OPD to outperform GRPO,
but none evaluate their claimed advantage over outcome-reward methods like GRPO in terms of
FLOPs (Appendix A ). They report sample efficiency ( Ko et al., 2026 ) , GPU-hours, or
wall-clock ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Rang et al., 2026 ) ; Zhao et al. (2026) reports FLOPs but only among OPD variants,
not against GRPO. Reported wall-clock or GPU-hour wins over GRPO also use different group sizes
for the two methods ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Tian et al., 2026 ) or leave it
unreported ( Rang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , so the gap is not
attributable to objective quality alone.
We isolate this confound by controlling group size and
characterizing external-teacher OPD through FLOPs, with a smaller-group-size ablation in
Appendix I .

blocks.en:
To our surprise, such intuition falls apart. Figure 2 shows the in-domain result: GRPO’s final
accuracy exceeds every OPD run’s peak in every cell at a smaller FLOP budget throughout. Although an OPD run sometimes briefly reaches GRPO’s early-training performance at lower compute early in the training, the advantage of GRPO over OPD widens as we use stronger and larger teachers. The OOD macro tells a different story (Figure 8 ). In the three cells where the teacher itself performs worst (the teacher mean@32 = 0 =0 column, plus the cell with student = 0 =0 and teacher ∈ ( 0 , 0.3 ] \in(0,$0.3$] ), every OPD run reaches a higher peak OOD accuracy than GRPO, the opposite of what the dense-signal motivation predicts; GRPO wins the other five cells. Moreover, OPD’s final OOD macro stays within 15 true % 15\text{true}\mathrm{\%} – 18 true % 18\text{true}\mathrm{\%} across all eight cells regardless of the training subset, while GRPO’s ranges from 11.9 true % 11.9\text{true}\mathrm{\%} to 20.5 true % 20.5\text{true}\mathrm{\%} . This suggests that part of what OPD learns from an external teacher does not depend on the training prompts; Appendix F examines this further.

blocks.en:
A highly cited work reports that GRPO-training the teacher before distillation can
help OPD ( Li et al., 2026 ) , but it establishes this claim on a limited experiment: running GRPO on Qwen3-4B-Base leads to a better teacher than Qwen3-4B (Non-thinking) when the student is Qwen3-1.7B-Base . We vary the teacher along three dimensions: 1) initialization — a base model or an external thinking model, 2) whether it is used as-is or first GRPO-trained on the task, and 3) its size — same or larger.

All experiments in this section use thinking mode. Families (i) and (iii) share the same GRPO recipe; the only difference is the response-length maximum ( 7168 7168 for base, 16 384 16\,384 for thinking; full hyperparameters in Table 2 ). We consider 4 domains in total: math on DAPO-Math-17K, code on LiveCodeBench-v1–v5, instruction following
on IFBench, and knowledge on MMLU-Pro. We experiment with 2-domain setting and 4-domain setting separately.
From Qwen3-4B-Base we train one GRPO expert on each single domain, each with its own hyperparameters (Table 11 ).
We build a data mix whose per-domain training instance count matches each individual
expert, and we compare four methods on it: (i) Joint GRPO (instance-mix) , which fills every batch with instances drawn proportionally from all domains at one shared batch size; (ii) Joint GRPO (batch-mix) , which draws each batch from each domain (each domain has its own batch size, notably a smaller batch on code domain) per step and interleaves domains across steps; (iii) Multi-teacher self-GRPO OPD , which routes each instance to the self-GRPO teacher of the corresponding domain and computes the reverse KL; (iv) External teacher OPD with a single 8 8 B-thinking teacher, the best-performing external teacher based on results from § 4 and § 5 . All OPD runs use rollout group size G = 1 G{=}1 unless otherwise noted. We run each method on 2 2 -domain (math + code) and 4 4 -domain mixes to show some scaling behavior; see Appendix J for more details.

blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
We give the first systematic, FLOPs-based characterization of strong-to-weak
OPD against GRPO, and identify when OPD is a promising post-training tool.
First, we find external teachers under vanilla reverse-KL broadly
lose to GRPO across our nine-axis ablation (§ 4 ); and we widely observe pathological behavior from the trained student with external teachers.
Second, through carefully studying the impact of GRPO on teachers, we realized the self-GRPO teacher (the student’s own GRPO checkpoint) is the only setup where the student consistently learns compute-efficiently and fully recovers teacher performance (§ 5 ). It matches GRPO’s performance at 50.0 50.0 × \times fewer FLOPs, replicated across domains, student sizes, and student families; the student’s best performance can even substantially exceed the teacher’s, calling for further study.
Third, multi-teacher OPD with self-GRPO teachers is a cheap
consolidation step (§ 6 ). It recovers every specialist for an extra 5.2 true % 5.2\text{true}\mathrm{\%} (2 domains) or 8.0 true % 8.0\text{true}\mathrm{\%} (4 domains) of specialist training FLOPs — cheaper
than joint GRPO on the same data; and substantially cheaper than
external-teacher OPD, which underperforms at 2 domains and collapses at 4.
Together, these results suggest OPD is not a straightforward replacement for GRPO, but it is an efficient way to fold many same-origin GRPO-trained specialists into a single generalist student.

blocks.en: We use the MMLU-Pro test set ( Wang et al., 2024 ) ( 11 904 11\,904 multiple-choice questions across 14 14 disciplines) as our knowledge-domain training source. The reward is binary: 1 1 if the model’s extracted answer matches the ground-truth option, 0 0 otherwise.

blocks.en: We use the MMLU-Pro test set rather than a separate training corpus because the multi-domain experiments (§ 6 ) are designed to test whether OPD can recover multiple specialist teachers simultaneously, not to produce a competitive MMLU-Pro score.

Evaluation uses the IFBench test split.

blocks.en: D.1 Training-data difficulty

blocks.en: This subsection documents the data construction and Qwen3-1.7B-Base results behind the difficulty grid in § 4.1 . The main in-domain and OOD findings are discussed there; here we provide construction details, the full per-cell OOD breakdown, and the 1.7B-specific observations that inform the broader study.
blocks.zh: 本分节将数据构造和Qwen3-1.7B-Base结果记录在了§ 4.1中难度网格后. 这里讨论的是主要的域内和OOD发现;这里我们提供构造细节,每个细胞OOD的全部分解,以及1.7B的具体观察,为更广泛的研究提供了参考.

blocks.en: We score every prompt in DAPO-Math-17K with mean@32 under both the Qwen3-1.7B-Base student and the Qwen3-4B thinking teacher, then bin along both axes ( = 0 =\!0 / > 0 >\!0 for the student; = 0 =\!0 , ( 0 , 0.3 ] (0,$0.3$] , ( 0.3 , 0.6 ] ($0.3$,$0.6$] , > 0.6 >\!$0.6$ for the teacher), yielding eight cells with matched train/in-domain-validation splits; for every subset, we keep the training set size to be 442 and validation set to be 128. We use a Qwen3-1.7B-Base student in no-think mode for the full eight-cell sweep; the OPD recipe in Yang et al. (2025) distills in either /think or /no_think mode, so no-think is a supported regime, and the 1.7 1.7 B pattern is if anything more severe than the 4 4 B headline.

The most striking feature of the 1.7 1.7 B difficulty grid is the behaviour on the OOD macro (AIME24/25 + AMC23; Figure 8 ). While GRPO’s OOD accuracy varies substantially across the eight cells, tracking which training subset it was given, OPD’s OOD macro is nearly constant at 15 true % 15\text{true}\mathrm{\%} – 18 true % 18\text{true}\mathrm{\%} regardless of the training cell. This constancy holds across all three teacher sizes ( 4 4 B, 8 8 B, 32 32 B) and persists even in the degenerate cell where both student and teacher score zero on the training prompts. In-domain, GRPO wins every cell over the best OPD results by a noticeable margin. On OOD, GRPO wins five of the eight cells, but OPD-4B and OPD-8B finish above GRPO in the three cells where the teacher itself performs badly (the entire teacher = 0 =0 column plus the student-zero/low-teacher cell). This reversal is the opposite of what the dense-signal motivation predicts: OPD gains its OOD advantage precisely where the teacher has the least task-solving information to contribute, suggesting that OPD’s OOD gain comes from the teacher’s general behavior rather than from the task-specific signal on the training prompts (see Appendix F ).

blocks.en: D.3 Batch size

blocks.en:
Batch size is another key hyperparameter for model tuning: it controls the noise level of gradient estimates. To isolate its effect while keeping the total training data fixed, we ran three batch-size
configurations – 64 64 for 200 200 steps, 128 128 for 100 100 steps,
and 256 256 at 50 50 steps – for GRPO and for OPD under each of the
three teacher sizes, all on DAPO-Math-17K with a Qwen3-1.7B-Base student in
no-think mode at learning rate 2 × 10 − 6 2\text{\times}{10}^{-6} (Figure 11 ). Smaller
batches help both methods: GRPO climbs from 19.5 19.5 to 20.9 20.9 to 24.0 24.0 (in-domain validation mean@16, %) as the batch shrinks from 256 256 to 128 128 to 64 64 ; OPD-4B follows the same staircase from 16.0 16.0 to 16.2 16.2 to 17.3 17.3 . The gain is roughly parallel, so the
relative ordering GRPO > > OPD holds at every batch size. For the two larger
teachers ( 8 8 B, 32 32 B) the pattern is noisier but still favours small
batch, and at no batch size does any OPD run overtake GRPO.

The ratio π θ / π old \pi_{\theta}/\pi_{\text{old}} corrects for off-policy sampling, and the per-token signal log ⁡ π old − log ⁡ π T \log\pi_{\text{old}}-\log\pi_{T} is negative where the teacher assigns higher probability than the rollout policy. This estimator needs only the student, rollout, and teacher log-probabilities at the sampled token, avoiding the top- k k renormalization entirely.

blocks.en: D.5 Thinking mode
blocks.zh: D. 5级 思维模式

blocks.en: Figure 13 isolates the effect of the teacher’s thinking mode. All runs use the same student ( Qwen3-1.7B-Base with OpenThoughts-3-SFT initialization) and the same data (DAPO-Math-17K); only the teacher decoding mode changes. In no-think mode (left panel), GRPO reaches roughly 19 true % 19\text{true}\mathrm{\%} OOD macro and the three OPD variants ( 4 4 B, 8 8 B, and 32 32 B teachers) cluster in a narrow 16 true % 16\text{true}\mathrm{\%} – 17.5 true % 17.5\text{true}\mathrm{\%} band, consistent with the main-text pattern. Switching to think mode (right panel) costs GRPO about 2.1 2.1 points, but the effect on OPD varies sharply with teacher size: OPD-8B loses a comparable 2.1 2.1 points and stays within 1.5 1.5 points of GRPO, whereas OPD-4B drops 8.2 8.2 points and OPD-32B drops 7.7 7.7 points, leaving both at roughly half the GRPO level.
blocks.zh: 图13隔离了老师思维模式的效果. 所有跑步都使用同名学生(用OpenThoughts-3-SFT初始化的Qwen3-1.7B-Base)和同名数据(DAPO-Math-17K);只有老师解码模式有变化. 在无思维模式( 左面板) 中, GRPO 大约达到 19 真% 19\ text{ true}\- mathrm{\%}} OOD宏和3个OPD变体(4 4 B,8 8 B,32 B教师)组合在一个狭义的16 real% 16\text{ true}\mathrm{\%} – 17.5 real% 17.5\text{ true}\mathrm{\%} 乐队,与正文模式一致. 切换到思维模式(右面板)成本为GRPO约2.1分,但对于OPD的影响随教师大小而大相径庭:OPD-8B损失了可比较的2.1. 1分并停留在GRPO的1.5分以内,而OPD-4B则下降8.2分,OPD-32B则下降7.7分,两者都大约为GRPO级别的一半.

blocks.en: Two observations follow. First, thinking mode hurts OPD more than GRPO across most teacher sizes, consistent with the hypothesis that long chains of thought amplify the distribution mismatch between student rollouts and teacher token-level supervision. Second, teacher capacity does not rescue the gap: the 32 32 B teacher fares worse than the 8 8 B teacher in think mode, not better, so the fragility is not a matter of teacher scale. We note that no-think and think runs differ in decoding temperature and prompt format, so the two panels are not a controlled comparison with each other; the GRPO-vs-OPD contrast within each panel is controlled.
blocks.zh: 以下两点意见。 首先,思维模式在大多数教师规模上比GRPO更会伤害OPD,这与长期思维链会扩大学生推出和教师象征性监督之间的分配不匹配的假设是一致的. 二,师资能力不能挽救差距:32个32个B的师资在思想模式下比8个B的师资票价差,并不好,所以脆弱性不是师资规模的问题. 我们注意到,不思考和思考在解码温度和即时格式上不同,因此两个面板不是相互控制的比较;每个面板内的GRPO-vs-OPD对比被控制.

blocks.en: D.6 Student initialization
blocks.zh: D.6 学生初始化

blocks.en: A natural hypothesis is that the base model must first learn to produce rollouts in the right format before OPD can distill from them effectively: if the student’s on-policy outputs are too far from the teacher’s distribution, token-level supervision may have little to work with. SFT cold-starting on high-quality traces (e.g. OpenThoughts-3) could therefore be important for OPD to succeed. We test this hypothesis at two student scales.
blocks.zh: 一个自然的假设是,基础模型必须首先学会以正确的格式推出,然后OPD才能有效地从中提炼出来:如果学生的政策产出与教师的分配太相去甚远,象征性的监督可能没有什么可配合的. 因此,在高质量痕迹(例如OpenThoughts-3)上进行SFT冷启动对于OPD的成功可能很重要. 我们用两个学生尺度来测试这个假设。

The negative result in § 4 is established on Qwen3-1.7B-Base . A natural concern is that the 1.7B student is simply
too small to benefit from a strong teacher and that the gap would close
at larger student scale. We test this by running the same external

larger teacher does not improve compute efficiency: the 32B teacher
curves sit close to (and sometimes below) the same-size teacher curves.
The negative result is not a small-student artifact.

However, this behavior is not inherent to dense per-token supervision. With the self-GRPO teacher (§ 5 ), OPD does not inflate length: the student ends at 3741 3741 tokens, close to GRPO’s 3813 3813 .
This inflation encodes pathological behavior of the model (Appendix E.2 ). We believe, following the dense-signal analogy of OPD, the problem is not the

the distillation. Developing such a diagnostic remains an open problem.

blocks.en: Like GRPO, reverse-KL OPD updates the student on its own rollouts, and the resulting spectral change stays within the same RLVR κ spec \kappa_{\mathrm{spec}} range regardless of the teacher (Table 10 ). If OPD shifts the student’s spectrum by only a small amount per unit of training compute, a teacher whose spectrum sits three orders of magnitude away is out of reach at any realistic compute budget: matching it would require an SFT-scale spectral move, which OPD’s gradient direction does not produce. A self-GRPO teacher sits in the same RLVR range as anything OPD can produce, so a small number of RLVR-magnitude steps is enough to reach it. The three-orders-of-magnitude κ spec \kappa_{\mathrm{spec}} gap in Table 10 is therefore a plausible mechanism for why external-teacher OPD is not compute-efficient on the training domain (§ 4 ).
